summary.text: A repeated-run-length analysis, seeded by finite checks at indices 8–11 and then propagated recursively, gives the coupled recurrences \(S_{n+1}=S_n+L_n\), \(L_{n+1}=L_n+C_n\), and \(C_{n+1}=C_n+S_{n-4}+3\). Choosing \(\lambda>1\) with \(\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1\), a positive weighted combination of these quantities and four lagged values of \(S_n+3\) scales exactly by \(\lambda\); comparison with \(S_n+3\) squeezes its nth roots to \(\lambda\), and the bounded ratio \(S_n/(S_n+3)\) removes the additive constant.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\mathcal R(w)\) denote the run-length encoding of a finite word \(w\): thus, if the maximal constant runs of \(w\) have lengths \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\), then \(\mathcal R(w)=(e_1,\ldots,e_r)\). Reversal of a word is denoted by \(w^{\rm rev}\), concatenation by juxtaposition, and \(|w|\) and \(\Sigma w\) denote its length and the sum of its entries.

Define the rows \(T_n\) by
\[
T_1=(1),\qquad T_2=(1),\qquad T_3=(2),
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
T_{n+1}=\mathcal R(T_n^{\rm rev})\,T_n.
\tag{1}
\]
The sequence in the question is
\[
S_n:=\Sigma T_n.
\]
(One may harmlessly put \(T_0\) equal to the empty word and \(S_0=0\).) We will prove that \(S_n^{1/n}\) converges. In fact, the proof identifies its limit as a particular real number \(\lambda>1\).

We first record elementary facts about run-length encoding. Every entry of \(\mathcal R(w)\) is positive, and
\[
\Sigma\mathcal R(w)=|w|.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the runs partition the positions of \(w\), and their lengths add up to the number of positions. Also,
\[
|\mathcal R(w)|=|\mathcal R(w^{\rm rev})|,
\qquad
\mathcal R(w^{\rm rev})=\mathcal R(w)^{\rm rev}.
\tag{3}
\]
The latter identity holds because reversal reverses the order of the maximal runs without changing any run length.

We shall repeatedly use the following append rule. If nonempty words \(v,w\) have unequal boundary entries (the last entry of \(v\) differs from the first entry of \(w\)), then
\[
\mathcal R(vw)=\mathcal R(v)\mathcal R(w).
\tag{4}
\]
If their boundary entries are equal, write the last run length of \(v\) as \(a\) and the first run length of \(w\) as \(b\). Then the two boundary runs merge, so
\[
\mathcal R(vw)
 =\mathcal R(v)\text{ with its last entry deleted},\ (a+b),\
   \mathcal R(w)\text{ with its first entry deleted}.
\tag{5}
\]
These statements follow directly by listing the maximal runs: away from the junction no run changes, while at the junction either nothing happens or precisely the two adjacent equal-valued runs coalesce. They also show that if a word is extended on the right, all entries of its run-length encoding except possibly its final entry remain unchanged.

Put
\[
L_n:=|T_n|,
\qquad
C_n:=|\mathcal R(T_n)|,
\qquad
D_n:=|\mathcal R^2(T_n)|,
\tag{6}
\]
where \(\mathcal R^2=\mathcal R\circ\mathcal R\). From (1), (2), and (3), for \(n\geq3\),
\[
S_{n+1}=S_n+L_n,
\tag{7}
\]
and
\[
L_{n+1}=L_n+C_n.
\tag{8}
\]
All entries of every \(T_n\) are positive: this is true of the three initial rows, and (1) preserves it because run lengths are positive. Consequently
\[
L_n\leq S_n.
\tag{9}
\]
It follows from (7) and the initial values that \(S_n>0\) for \(n\geq1\), and \(S_n\) is nondecreasing from \(n=2\) onward. It also follows that
\[
S_{n+1}\leq2S_n\quad(n\geq1),
\tag{10}
\]
with the cases \(n=1,2\) checked from \(S_1=1,S_2=1,S_3=2\), and the later cases following from (7) and (9). Thus \(S_n\leq2^n\), although the sharper structure below is what will give convergence.

We next derive a recurrence for \(C_n\). Direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_4&=(1,2),\\
T_5&=(1,1,1,2),\\
T_6&=(1,3,1,1,1,2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The final four entries of \(T_n\) are
\[
(1,1,1,2)\qquad(n\geq5).
\tag{12}
\]
This is true at \(n=5\), and is preserved because \(T_n\) is a suffix of \(T_{n+1}\) by (1). Similarly, from \(T_6\) onward the final five entries are
\[
(3,1,1,1,2).
\tag{13}
\]
Hence \(T_n^{\rm rev}\) starts with \((2,1,1,1,3)\) for \(n\geq6\), so its run-length encoding starts with \((1,3)\). By (1), therefore,
\[
T_n\text{ starts with }(1,3)\qquad(n\geq6).
\tag{14}
\]
In particular, the first run of \(T_n\) has length one.

Now apply \(\mathcal R\) to (1). The left block \(\mathcal R(T_n^{\rm rev})\) ends in the length of the first run of \(T_n\), which is \(1\) by (14), and the right block \(T_n\) begins with \(1\). Thus the last run of the left block and first run of the right block merge. The number of runs in a concatenation with such a merge is the sum of the numbers of runs of the two blocks minus one. By (3), the number of runs in \(\mathcal R(T_n^{\rm rev})\) is \(D_n\). We obtain
\[
C_{n+1}+1=D_n+C_n\qquad(n\geq6),
\tag{15}
\]
or equivalently
\[
C_{n+1}=C_n+D_n-1.
\tag{16}
\]

The key structural assertion is
\[
D_n=S_{n-4}+4\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{17}
\]
We now prove it in detail.

Reverse the rows and set
\[
U_n:=T_n^{\rm rev},
\qquad
R_{1,n}:=\mathcal R(U_n),
\qquad
R_{2,n}:=\mathcal R(R_{1,n}),
\qquad
R_{3,n}:=\mathcal R(R_{2,n}),
\qquad
R_{4,n}:=\mathcal R(R_{3,n}).
\tag{18}
\]
Reversing (1) and using (3) gives
\[
U_{n+1}=U_n\,R_{1,n}^{\rm rev}\qquad(n\geq3).
\tag{19}
\]
Thus every \(U_n\) is a prefix of every later \(U_m\).

For \(k\geq4\), \(U_k\) starts with \(2,1\): its first entry is the final entry \(2\) of \(T_k\), and (12), together with the direct case \(k=4\), gives the following entry \(1\). Define \(Y_k\) by replacing this initial \(2\) in \(U_k\) with \(6\). Thus, if \(U_k=(2)q\), then
\[
Y_k=(6)q.
\tag{20}
\]
Because the following entry is \(1\), both the initial \(2\) and the replacement \(6\) form isolated runs of length one. Therefore
\[
\mathcal R(Y_k)=\mathcal R(U_k)=R_{1,k}.
\tag{21}
\]
Equation (19), with only that unchanged first entry replaced, now yields
\[
Y_{k+1}=Y_k\,\mathcal R(Y_k)^{\rm rev}
\qquad(k\geq4).
\tag{22}
\]
Thus the words \(Y_k\) obey exactly the same append evolution as the words \(U_k\), but start with \(6\) instead of \(2\). Moreover,
\[
\Sigma Y_k=\Sigma U_k+4=S_k+4.
\tag{23}
\]

We next prove
\[
R_{3,n}=Y_{n-4}\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{24}
\]
The first four cases are finite run-length computations. They are included explicitly because they initialize the later structural induction. From the row recurrence one obtains
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_8={}&(2,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,3,1),\\
R_{1,8}={}&(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1),\\
R_{2,8}={}&(1,1,1,1,1,1,4),\\
R_{3,8}={}&(6,1)=Y_4;
\end{aligned}
\tag{25}
\]
for \(n=9\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{1,9}&=(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,1),\\
R_{2,9}&=(1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,6),\\
R_{3,9}&=(6,1,1,1)=Y_5;
\end{aligned}
\tag{26}
\]
for \(n=10\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{1,10}&=(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1),\\
R_{2,10}&=(1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1,6),\\
R_{3,10}&=(6,1,1,1,3,1)=Y_6;
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
\]
and for \(n=11\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{1,11}={}&(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,1,1,5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1),\\
R_{2,11}={}&(1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1,5,1,3,1,1,1,6),\\
R_{3,11}={}&(6,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1)=Y_7.
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Every displayed identity is obtained simply by grouping adjacent equal entries into maximal runs. Notice in particular that \(|R_{1,11}|=36\).

It remains to propagate (24) beyond \(11\). For this we need enough fixed boundary information to control all mergers in repeated run-length encodings. The relevant stabilized prefix is
\[
P=(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1).
\tag{29}
\]
For every \(n\geq11\), both \(T_n\) and \(R_{1,n}\) begin with \(P\).

Here is why. The assertion is directly visible in the computed words at \(n=11\). Since \(U_{11}\) is a prefix of every \(U_n\), formulae (4)–(5) show that \(R_{1,n}=\mathcal R(U_n)\) agrees with \(R_{1,11}\) except possibly at the final run contributed by \(U_{11}\). Since \(|R_{1,11}|=36\), its first seventeen entries, namely \(P\), cannot be affected by that possible final merger. Thus every \(R_{1,n}\), \(n\geq11\), begins with \(P\). On the other hand, for \(n\geq12\), equation (1) says that \(T_n\) begins with \(\mathcal R(U_{n-1})=R_{1,n-1}\), and this block has at least seventeen entries. Hence \(T_n\) begins with \(P\); the case \(n=11\) was already computed.

Reversing this fixed prefix gives fixed suffixes of \(U_n\). In particular, for \(n\geq11\), its final sixteen entries are
\[
(7,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1),
\tag{30}
\]
and its final seventeen entries are
\[
(1,7,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1).
\tag{31}
\]
Run-length encoding (30) gives
\[
(1,5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1).
\tag{32}
\]
The extra leading entry in (31) is \(1\), whereas (30) begins with \(7\), so there is no merger at that boundary. It follows that the final ten entries of \(R_{1,n}\) are exactly the word in (32):
\[
R_{1,n}\text{ ends in }(1,5,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1).
\tag{33}
\]
In particular, it ends in six consecutive \(1\)'s. Encoding (33) gives
\[
(1,1,1,1,6).
\tag{34}
\]
Even if the first entry displayed in (33) merges with what precedes it, only the first output in (34) can change. Therefore the last four entries of \(R_{2,n}\) are
\[
(1,1,1,6).
\tag{35}
\]
These observations also show that all the words under discussion are long enough for the stated deletions of final entries.

We now derive the successor formulas. Since \(T_n\) begins with \(1\) for \(n\geq6\), the last entry of \(U_n\) is \(1\). The last entry of \(R_{1,n}\) is the length of the first run of \(T_n\), hence also \(1\). Thus in (19), the last run of \(U_n\) merges with the first run of \(R_{1,n}^{\rm rev}\).

The last run of \(U_n\) has length \(1\): equivalently, the final entry of \(R_{1,n}\) is \(1\). The first run of \(R_{1,n}^{\rm rev}\) has length equal to the final entry of \(R_{2,n}\), which is \(6\) by (35). Hence the merged run has length \(7\). Applying (5) to (19) gives, for \(n\geq11\),
\[
R_{1,n+1}
=(R_{1,n}\text{ without its last entry})\,(7)\,
 (R_{2,n}\text{ without its last entry})^{\rm rev}.
\tag{36}
\]

We next encode (36). By (33), deleting the final entry from \(R_{1,n}\) leaves five consecutive final \(1\)'s, preceded by \(3\). Consequently
\[
\mathcal R(R_{1,n}\text{ without its last entry})
=(R_{2,n}\text{ without its last entry})\,(5).
\tag{37}
\]
The final entry of the first block in (36) is \(1\), the middle entry is \(7\), and by (35) the first entry of the final reversed block is also \(1\). Both boundaries are therefore unequal. Using (4), (3), and \(\mathcal R((7))=(1)\), we get
\[
R_{2,n+1}
=(R_{2,n}\text{ without its last entry})\,(5,1)\,
 \mathcal R(R_{2,n}\text{ without its last entry})^{\rm rev}.
\tag{38}
\]

Finally encode (38). By (35), after deleting the final \(6\), the word \(R_{2,n}\) ends in three consecutive \(1\)'s. Thus its last entry is \(1\), different from the first entry \(5\) of the middle block. Also, the final entry of \((5,1)\) is \(1\). The first entry of the last block in (38) is the final run length of \(R_{2,n}\) with its last entry deleted; this is at least \(3\), because that word ends in at least three \(1\)'s. Hence the second boundary is unequal as well. Formula (4) therefore applies at both boundaries. Since \(\mathcal R(5,1)=(1,1)\), we obtain
\[
R_{3,n+1}=R_{3,n}\,R_{4,n}^{\rm rev}
\qquad(n\geq11).
\tag{39}
\]
For completeness, one can see the cancellation in (39) directly. If \(E=\mathcal R(R_{2,n}\text{ without its last entry})\), then (35) implies
\[
R_{3,n}=E(1),
\qquad
R_{4,n}=\mathcal R(E)(1),
\]
while (38) gives
\[
R_{3,n+1}=E(1,1)\mathcal R(E)^{\rm rev}
=R_{3,n}R_{4,n}^{\rm rev}.
\]
The nonmerger facts just proved justify each displayed concatenation.

We can now finish the induction for (24). It holds for \(n=8,9,10,11\) by (25)–(28). Suppose \(n\geq11\) and \(R_{3,n}=Y_{n-4}\). Then \(R_{4,n}=\mathcal R(Y_{n-4})\), so (39) and (22) give
\[
R_{3,n+1}
=Y_{n-4}\mathcal R(Y_{n-4})^{\rm rev}
=Y_{n-3}.
\]
Thus (24) holds for every \(n\geq8\).

We now translate (24) into (17). By (2), the length of a run-length encoding equals the sum of the entries of the next encoding. Reversal does not affect the number of runs. Therefore
\[
D_n=|\mathcal R^2(T_n)|=\Sigma R_{3,n}.
\tag{40}
\]
Using (24) and (23),
\[
D_n=\Sigma Y_{n-4}=S_{n-4}+4,
\]
as claimed.

Substituting (17) into (16), we have obtained the exact system
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
S_{n+1}&=S_n+L_n,\\
L_{n+1}&=L_n+C_n,\\
C_{n+1}&=C_n+S_{n-4}+3
\end{aligned}}
\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{41}
\]
This finite-dimensional delayed linear system determines the exponential rate.

Choose a real number \(\lambda\in(1,2)\) satisfying
\[
\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1.
\tag{42}
\]
Such a number exists by the intermediate value theorem: the continuous function
\[
g(x)=x^4(x-1)^3-1
\]
has \(g(1)=-1\) and \(g(2)=15\). Put \(q=\lambda-1>0\), and write
\[
B_n:=S_n+3.
\]
Define the positive linear functional
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_n={}&B_n+q^{-1}L_n+q^{-2}C_n
 +qB_{n-1}+\lambda qB_{n-2}\\
&\quad+\lambda^2qB_{n-3}+\lambda^3qB_{n-4}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{43}
\]
All coefficients are positive. We claim that
\[
\Phi_{n+1}=\lambda\Phi_n\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{44}
\]
To verify this, use (41), equivalently
\[
B_{n+1}=B_n+L_n,
\quad L_{n+1}=L_n+C_n,
\quad C_{n+1}=C_n+B_{n-4}.
\tag{45}
\]
Substitute (45) into (43) with \(n+1\) in place of \(n\), and group coefficients of \(L_n,C_n,B_n,B_{n-1},\ldots,B_{n-4}\). The coefficients of \(L_n\) and \(C_n\) agree with those in \(\lambda\Phi_n\) because
\[
\lambda q^{-1}=q^{-1}+1,
\qquad
\lambda q^{-2}=q^{-2}+q^{-1},
\tag{46}
\]
which are immediate from \(\lambda=1+q\). The shifted \(B\)-terms telescope through the coefficients
\[
q,\ \lambda q,\ \lambda^2q,\ \lambda^3q.
\]
The final coefficient agrees because (42) says
\[
q^{-2}=\lambda^4q.
\tag{47}
\]
These identities establish (44). Induction now gives
\[
\Phi_n=\lambda^{n-8}\Phi_8\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{48}
\]
Also \(\Phi_8>0\), since every term in (43) is nonnegative and \(B_8=S_8+3>0\).

We compare \(\Phi_n\) with \(B_n\). First,
\[
S_n\leq\Phi_n,
\tag{49}
\]
because the first term in \(\Phi_n\) is \(S_n+3\) and all remaining terms are nonnegative.

For the reverse comparison, recall that \(S_n\) is nondecreasing for \(n\geq2\). For \(n\geq8\), therefore,
\[
B_{n-j}\leq B_n\qquad(1\leq j\leq4).
\tag{50}
\]
Furthermore \(L_n\leq S_n\leq B_n\) by (9), and
\[
C_n=|\mathcal R(T_n)|\leq|T_n|=L_n\leq S_n\leq B_n,
\tag{51}
\]
because every run has positive length, so a word cannot have more runs than positions. Consequently
\[
\Phi_n\leq K B_n\qquad(n\geq8),
\tag{52}
\]
where the positive constant
\[
K=1+q^{-1}+q^{-2}+q+\lambda q+\lambda^2q+\lambda^3q
\tag{53}
\]
is independent of \(n\).

Combining (48), (49), and (52) yields two-sided exponential bounds for \(B_n=S_n+3\):
\[
\frac{\Phi_8}{K}\lambda^{n-8}
\leq S_n+3
\leq (\Phi_8+3)\lambda^{n-8}
\qquad(n\geq8).
\tag{54}
\]
For the upper bound, (49) and (48) give \(S_n\leq\Phi_8\lambda^{n-8}\); adding \(3\) and using \(\lambda^{n-8}\geq1\) gives the stated right side. The lower bound follows by inserting (48) into (52). Both constants \(\Phi_8/K\) and \(\Phi_8+3\) are positive.

Taking positive real \(n\)-th roots in (54), we use the elementary limits
\[
c^{1/n}\longrightarrow1\quad(c>0),
\qquad
\left(\lambda^{n-8}\right)^{1/n}
=\lambda^{(n-8)/n}\longrightarrow\lambda.
\tag{55}
\]
The squeeze theorem gives
\[
(S_n+3)^{1/n}\longrightarrow\lambda.
\tag{56}
\]

It remains only to remove the added constant \(3\). Since \(S_n\geq1\) for \(n\geq1\),
\[
\frac14\leq\frac{S_n}{S_n+3}\leq1.
\tag{57}
\]
Taking \(n\)-th roots and using \((1/4)^{1/n}\to1\), another application of the squeeze theorem gives
\[
\left(\frac{S_n}{S_n+3}\right)^{1/n}\longrightarrow1.
\tag{58}
\]
Because all quantities are positive,
\[
S_n^{1/n}=(S_n+3)^{1/n}
\left(\frac{S_n}{S_n+3}\right)^{1/n}.
\tag{59}
\]
Combining (56), (58), and (59), we conclude that
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} S_n^{1/n}=\lambda},
\]
where \(\lambda\in(1,2)\) satisfies \(\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1\). In particular, the limit in the conjecture exists.
